newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian anti-kidnap chief arrested-for kidnapping.
newsitem.headline: Colombian anti-kidnap chief arrested-for kidnapping.

text.p: The deputy director of Colombia's elite anti-kidnap squad has been arrested and charged with abducting two people, a senior police chief told local television on Friday.

Maj. Manuel de Jesus Lozada, second-in-command of the country's crack GAULA force, is accused of being behind the forced disappearance of a man and a woman in Cali, Colombia's second largest city, in 1995.
"We're charging him with falsifying documents and some disappearances," Gen. Luis Ernesto Gilibert, the deputy head of the National Police told the AMPM TV news programme.

Under Colombian law, "disappearances" are classified as abductions. Gilibert did not say when Lozada had been arrested or whether the bodies of his two victims had ever re-appeared. A police spokesman in Bogota was not available for comment.

Statistics on the number of forced disappearances in Colombia are not readily available. In the past both the police and army have been accused of "disappearing" suspected leftist rebels and their sympathisers. Illegal right-wing paramilitary groups are also frequently blamed for "disappearing" left-wing rivals.

The GAULA anti-kidnap force is a combined police and army unit trained by the British army's Special Air Service (SAS). It is in the front line in the fight against the rising tide of kidnaps carried out in this Andean nation.

Last year there were more than 1,400 reported abductions in Colombia, making it the undisputed kidnap capital of the world. One Western defence official believes the real number of abductions is up to four times higher, but says relatives are afraid to inform the police in case their loved ones are harmed in a bungled rescue attempt.
More than half the kidnaps in 1996 were atttributed to leftist guerrillas who fund their activities with ransom payments.
